column2: The prior Mizpah oath prohibits each Israelite from giving his daughter to Benjamin as a wife; none of us renders the distributed negative.
The selected destination includes both Mizpah and Bethel, with sitting before God until evening, raised voices and great weeping.
column3: Bitterly is the inherited idiomatic expression for the intense wept-a-great-weeping construction; the Greek adjective itself is great, not bitter.

column2: The prayer asks why one tribe should be visited today in Israel; the repeated Israel and selected passive verb remain.
column3: Visited for episkeptomai is unresolved in this casualty/muster context; missing or punished would each interpret the clause more specifically and are not silently substituted.

column2: Next-day early rising leads to building an altar and whole burnt offerings of deliverance, consistent with the selected construction at 20:26.
column3: No conjunction introduces a separate peace-offering category in the Greek; the unusual genitive expression remains provisional.

column2: The assembly asks who failed to come from all Israel's tribes, explaining the prior great oath and emphatic death penalty for absence at Mizpah.
The people are comforted concerning their brother Benjamin and lament a tribe's removal; the selected comfort verb remains visible beside the troubling context.
column3: Comforted for parakaleo is provisional; moved to pity or relented may fit contextual usage but requires explicit lexical assessment rather than harmonization.

column2: The survivors' need for wives conflicts with the oath by the Lord against giving daughters; both sides of that stated dilemma remain.
The question asks which one tribe failed to come, then behold identifies no man from Jabesh-gilead in camp/assembly; the geographic shift is not corrected.
Inspection confirms with a second behold that none of Jabesh-gilead's inhabitants is there; the repeated discovery remains.
The congregation sends twelve thousand mighty men with orders to strike all inhabitants, women and people; no softer task replaces the violent command.
The ban targets every male and every woman who has known a male's bed; the sexual-status criterion is retained.
column3: Put under the ban expresses anathema-language whose destructive force is clear from the preceding order; it is not a merely social exclusion.

column2: Four hundred young virgins are identified by the repeated no-sexual-knowledge wording and taken to Shiloh in Canaan; the count and destination remain.
The whole congregation sends and speaks to Benjamin at Rimmon, inviting peace; word is an English supplied object of the sending.
Benjamin returns and receives the Jabesh-gilead women, and the selected conclusion says this pleased them; a not-enough statement is not imported.
The people are comforted concerning Benjamin because the Lord made the breach; divine agency remains explicit.
column3: As at verse 6, the contextual sense of parakaleo needs review; the inherited wording is not treated as a settled emotional interpretation.

column2: The elders again ask about wives for the remaining men because Benjamin's women have been made to disappear; the passive destruction expression remains.
A preserved inheritance and emphatic refusal to blot out a tribe are both asserted; certainly not voices ou me.
Their inability to give wives is explained by the sworn curse on whoever gives one to Benjamin; the quoted oath remains inside the elders' speech.
The recurring feast at Shiloh is located north of Bethel, eastward on the Shechem road, and south of Lebanon, of Lebona; both selected final names remain.
column3: The Lebanon/Lebona relation is geographically and syntactically difficult; no apparatus or alternative witness collation has resolved it here.

column2: The command sends Benjamin across to ambush in vineyards, retaining the explicit planned concealment.
Propose behold after Watch to retain idou before the women's emergence; the repeated Shiloh, dances, each man's seizure and return to Benjamin remain.
column3: The futures are rendered as commands in the instruction sequence. Seize is coercive abduction, without language implying the women consented.

column2: The proposed response to fathers or brothers retains mercy, the failure to take wives in war, the denial that they gave them, and the affirmative you committed an offence.
column3: The final clause is not negated to fit a familiar oath explanation. Pronoun shifts and the precise reference of at that time remain unresolved in the selected wording.

column2: Benjamin follows the plan, taking the number of wives from dancers they snatched away, then returns, builds cities and settles; coercive agency remains explicit.
Departure is repeated, first to tribe and kindred and then to inheritance; the source's distributed each-man wording remains.
The closing no-king notice says each did what was right in his own eyes; right renders euthes here, distinct from good at 17:6.
